Ribosome. These are the cellular machines that synthesize proteins by translating messenger RNA into chains of amino acids. You find ribosomes in all cells, both prokaryotic and eukaryotic. They're made up of ribosomal RNA called rRNA and ribosomal proteins assembled into two subunits—a large subunit and a small subunit. In bacteria these are called the seventy-S ribosome, while in eukaryotes they're the eighty-S ribosome. The ribosome is where genetic instructions are converted into functional proteins.

A ribosome reads codons on messenger RNA in sequence from the five-prime end to the three-prime end. As it reads, transfer RNA molecules called tRNA bring amino acids to match each codon through anticodon-codon pairing. The ribosome catalyzes the formation of peptide bonds between these amino acids, linking them into a growing chain.

There are two locations for ribosomes in the cell. Free ribosomes floating in the cytoplasm make proteins destined for the cytoplasm itself. Bound ribosomes attached to the endoplasmic reticulum make secreted proteins and proteins that will be inserted into membranes. These protein destinations are determined during translation by signal sequences that direct proteins destined for secretion to the rough endoplasmic reticulum.

Ribosomal RNA is synthesized in the nucleolus and combined with ribosomal proteins in the cytoplasm to assemble functional ribosomes. The ribosome can add hundreds of amino acids per minute. Importantly, the ribosomal RNA itself actually catalyzes peptide bond formation—it's a ribozyme. This highlights the central role of RNA in early cellular chemistry. Most antibiotics work by targeting bacterial ribosomes, exploiting structural differences that distinguish them from eukaryotic ribosomes.
